summary: A statement from the Internet Architecture Board arguing that changing the addresses of hosts and subnets, called renumbering, will become more common, so solutions that make it easier should be developed and deployed. It also touches on how DNS names relate to IP addresses.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains why organizations may need to change their network addresses and why the work is difficult. It recommends using stable domain names in place of stored IP addresses and developing tools to automate address changes.

questions: why use domain names instead of ip addresses
what did the iab recommend about renumbering
subtitle: The IAB urges network designers to make changing IP addresses easier.

tldr.problem: Changing host and subnet IP addresses is costly and error-prone, and the IAB expected renumbering to become more common.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends relying on domain names, avoiding hardcoded addresses and developing tools such as DHCP and authenticated dynamic DNS updates.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational set of recommendations that also calls for renumbering experience to be shared and documented.

today: RFC 1900 is Informational and has no later obsoleting or updating RFC listed in the unit metadata. Its discussion of tools and work in progress describes the period in which it was written.

sections.title: Why Networks Need Renumbering
sections.content:
Renumbering means changing the IP addressing information for a host or subnet. It may be needed when a host moves to another subnet, when an overloaded subnet is split, or when an organization changes its address plan.

The RFC explains that organizations using address blocks from a service provider may need new addresses when they change providers. Without renumbering, they could have limited connectivity or face extra costs related to routing information. The RFC describes renumbering as costly, tedious and error-prone, with few widely deployed tools and little shared documentation.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks may need new IP addresses when computers move, networks change or a provider changes. The RFC says making those changes was difficult and lacked good tools.

sections.title: Domain Names and IP Addresses
sections.content:
An IP address identifies a network interface, while the Domain Name System (DNS) associates readable names with IP addresses. The RFC says the DNS name space is independent of the address space. A DNS name may reflect ownership or function, while an IP address change is a technical change.

Using Fully Qualified Domain Names (FQDNs) defers the lookup of an IP address until run time. The RFC says names are expected to last longer than addresses and that dynamic DNS updates are needed when both names and addresses are assigned dynamically.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain name can stay the same when a host's IP address changes. Looking up the address when needed can limit how many settings must change during renumbering.

sections.title: Recommendations for Easier Changes
sections.content:
The IAB recommends minimizing IP addresses stored in human-maintained configuration, using FQDNs where possible, and avoiding addresses hardcoded in applications. Other files that map names to addresses should be avoided except for DNS configuration. If an older application requires addresses, its configuration can be generated from a file of domain names by looking up those names in DNS.

The RFC discourages licensing based on a host's IP address and calls for a toolkit to automate host renumbering. It identifies DHCP, dynamic router discovery, service location and authenticated dynamic DNS updates as parts of such a toolkit. It also encourages sharing and documenting experience.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB recommends storing names instead of fixed IP addresses where possible. It also calls for tools that can update addresses and network settings automatically.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says renumbering is believed to be compatible with the Internet security architecture if addresses do not change during the lifetime of a security association.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says an address should not change while a security association is active.
